title: Kerala's Chokramudi Hills Open for Tourists as Neelakurinji Blooms Paint Munnar Blue
excerpt: The once-in-12-years Neelakurinji flowering season has begun in Munnar's high ranges, with the spectacular mass bloom of Strobilanthes kunthiana expected to peak in September and October.
body:
• The Neelakurinji (Strobilanthes kunthiana) has begun its once-in-12-years flowering cycle in the high ranges of Munnar and the Nilgiris in southern India.
  • The mass bloom is expected to peak in September and October 2026, transforming hillsides into a sea of purplish-blue flowers at altitudes between 1,300 and 2,400 meters.
  • Chokramudi Hills, a major Neelakurinji site outside Eravikulam National Park, faces threats from encroachment — illegal construction in Bison Valley has destroyed thousands of plants.
  • Neelakurinji was listed under Schedule III of the Wildlife Protection Act in January 2023, making its destruction punishable by a ₹25,000 fine and up to three years of imprisonment.

A 12-Year Wait Ends

The high ranges of Munnar in Kerala's Idukki district are witnessing the early stages of one of nature's rarest spectacles. The Neelakurinji — Strobilanthes kunthiana — has begun its gregarious flowering, an event that occurs only once every 12 years. The last major bloom was in 2014, and botanical enthusiasts have been counting down to this season.

According to field reports from August 2026, Strobilanthes sessilis has already burst into bloom near Gudalur along the hilly stretches leading to Nadukani in the Nilgiris, with early sightings also appearing in pockets of Kerala's Idukki district. The Munnar high ranges are at the very beginning of their kurinji season.

Where and When to See the Bloom

The widespread mass blossoming is expected in September and October, when Strobilanthes kunthiana — the species globally renowned as the Neelakurinji — is slated to carpet the hillsides in purplish-blue. The flowering is expected at Munnar, Lockhart Gap, and areas within Tata tea plantations in Idukki district. Key viewing locations include Eravikulam National Park at Rajamala, Kolukkumala, Kottakamboor, Vattavada, and Kanthalloor.

The flowers thrive naturally at altitudes between 1,300 and 2,400 meters within the shola-grasslands of the Western Ghats. The Nilgiri hills — literally meaning "Blue Mountains" — historically owe their name to this phenomenon, with the blossoms transforming entire mountainsides into a sea of blue.

Revenue, forest, and tourism officials are holding meetings to organize crowd control during the flowering season. Eravikulam National Park typically restricts daily visitors to around 3,500, with tickets available online.

Threats to Chokramudi

Chokramudi Hills, one of the major Neelakurinji areas outside Eravikulam National Park, faces a serious conservation challenge. Large-scale illegal constructions upstream of Bison Valley in Idukki have led to the destruction of thousands of Neelakurinji plants, threatening the bloom that was expected for 2026.

Over the decades, human settlements and commercial plantations have occupied a significant portion of the natural shola habitat. To safeguard this biodiversity, the Kurinjimala Sanctuary was established across the Kottakamboor and Vattavada villages in Idukki. In January 2023, the Ministry of Environment, Forest, and Climate Change listed Neelakurinji under Schedule III of the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972, making the uprooting or destruction of these plants punishable by a ₹25,000 fine and up to three years of imprisonment.

Cultural Significance

The flowering of the kurinji holds profound traditional significance for indigenous communities of the region. The Muthuvas of Munnar and the Todas of the Nilgiris have cultural practices tied to the 12-year blooming cycle. The event also draws the endangered Nilgiri Tahr — a mountain goat native to these ranges — which can be spotted ambling through the flower-covered hillsides during the bloom.

Planning a Visit

Travelers should note that the peak bloom is expected from mid-September through October. Munnar is accessible by road from Kochi airport (approximately 140 km) or Angamaly railway station (approximately 108 km). Accommodation ranges from luxury plantation stays to budget guesthouses. Visitors to Eravikulam National Park should book tickets online in advance, as capacity is limited. Some viewing areas like Yellapatty require trekking about 4 km over steep terrain, while other spots are accessible by road near Vattavada.
